title: Algorithms
body_md:
Given $p,\mathcal I,\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf L,\Delta$ and
$\varepsilon$, an algorithm $A$ adaptively queries $\mathcal O_f$
and outputs $\widehat x_A(f)\in\mathbb R$.
Its queries and output depend on the preceding oracle responses
and, if randomized, an internal random seed independent of $f$.
The algorithm succeeds if $|f'(\widehat x_A(f))|<\varepsilon$.
head: manual

label: lmm:normal
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: \bf Normalization

label: thm:randomized-derivative-lower-bound
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: \bf Randomized derivative-only lower bound

label: lem:hard-family-properties
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:hard-family-properties}
For $0<\varepsilon\le(8K)^{-1}$, the preceding construction
satisfies $m\ge4$ and $m\ge(4K\varepsilon)^{-1}$.
Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin = *,itemsep=2pt, parsep=0pt, topsep=3pt]
    \item \textbf{Regularity and initial gap.}
    For every $j\in[m]$,
    $f_j\in\mathcal F_{\mathcal I,\boldsymbol\beta}(\mathbf1,1)$.

    \item \textbf{Indistinguishability.}
    For every $j\in[m]$ and $x\notin H_j$,
    $\mathcal O_{f_j}^{1:p}(x)=(-\delta/K,0,\ldots,0)$,
    where $\delta/K\ge2\varepsilon$.

    \item \textbf{Localization of stationary points.}
    The sets $H_1,\ldots,H_m$ are pairwise disjoint.
    Every $\varepsilon$-stationary point of $f_j$ belongs to $H_j$,
    and each connected component of $H_j$ contains a stationary point.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: \bf Properties of the hard family

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $S:=\min_{r\in\mathcal I}
L_r^{\frac{1}{r+\beta_r}}\Delta^{\frac{r+\beta_r-1}{r+\beta_r}}$.
Rescaling Lemma~\ref{lem:hard-family-properties} gives
$m=\Omega_p(S/\varepsilon)$ instances with disjoint stationary
regions and a common oracle response outside the hidden regions.

Fix a random seed and consider the common-response execution.
For $N<m$, at most $N$ regions are queried.
All untouched instances produce the same output, which succeeds
on at most one of them.
Averaging over the seed therefore gives
\[
\frac12
\le \frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m
\mathbb P\!\left(
|F_j'(\widehat x_A(F_j))|<\varepsilon
\right)
\le \frac{N+1}{m}.
\]
Hence $N\ge m/2-1=\Omega_p(S/\varepsilon)$.
The bound holds for $\mathcal O^{1:p}$ and thus for $\mathcal O^1$.
head: environment

label: thm:deterministic-derivative-jet-lower
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: \bf Deterministic derivative-only lower bound

label: lmm:derivative-hard-family
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lmm:derivative-hard-family}
For $K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}$ sufficiently large, every function $f_S$
constructed above satisfies the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin = *,itemsep=2pt, parsep=0pt, topsep=3pt]
    \item \textbf{Regularity and initial gap.}
    The function $f_S\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ is nonincreasing and
    bounded below, with $f_S(0)=\Delta$.
    Moreover, $[f_S^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}\le L_r$ for every $1\le r\le p$,
    and $f_S(0)-\inf f_S\le4\varepsilon h|S|\le\Delta$.

    \item \textbf{Oracle values.}
    For every $s\in S$ and $|x-s|<\frac h2$,
    $f_S'(x)=-2\varepsilon$ and
    $f_S^{(j)}(x)=0$ for $2\le j\le p$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: \bf Properties of the hard family

title: Proof
body_md:
The accuracy assumption ensures $\varepsilon h\le\frac{\Delta}{16}$.
Fix a deterministic algorithm and answer every query with
$f'=-2\varepsilon$ and $f^{(j)}=0$ for $2\le j\le p$.
If it outputs within $Q$ queries, let $S$ contain the origin,
its query locations, and its output.
                                                                    
                          
                               
For $Q<\frac{\Delta}{16\varepsilon h}$,
we have $4\varepsilon h|S|<\Delta$.
Lemma~\ref{lmm:derivative-hard-family} supplies an admissible $f_S$
that reproduces all simulated replies.
Determinism forces the same execution that the output has derivative
$-2\varepsilon$, or the algorithm exceeds $Q$ queries.
Thus the complexity is at least $\frac{\Delta}{16\varepsilon h}$ and
substituting $h$ gives the claimed bound.
The full proof is deferred to
Appendix~\ref{app:deterministic-derivative-lower}.
head: environment

label: thm:randomized-derivative-upper-bound
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: \bf Derivative-only upper bounds

label: lmm:derivative-interpolation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lmm:derivative-interpolation}
Suppose $[f^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}\le1$ and write $\nu:=r+\beta_r$.
Given an interval $I=[a,b]$ and an accuracy $\delta>0$,
a deterministic algorithm uses
$O_{r,\beta_r}\!\left(
1+|I|\delta^{-\frac{1}{\nu-1}}\right)$
derivative queries to construct a continuous piecewise polynomial
$P_\delta$ satisfying
$\|f'-P_\delta\|_{\infty,I}\le\delta$.
Moreover, $P_\delta(a)=f'(a)$ and $P_\delta(b)=f'(b)$.
head: environment
name: \bf Approximation

title: Proof
body_md:
The initial gap and $T = \frac{2}{\varepsilon}$ imply that $\int_0^T(f'(x)+\varepsilon)\,dx\ge1$.
In deterministic mode, the approximation $P$ must cross
$-\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$, and its error bound in Lemma~\ref{lmm:derivative-interpolation} certifies stationarity
at every crossing.

In randomized mode, the set $G:=\{x\in[0,T]:f'(x)>-\varepsilon\}$
has weight at least $1$, while its complement has weight at most $2T$.
Thus each sample hits $G$ with probability at least
$\frac{1}{1+4/\varepsilon}$.
The prescribed number of samples succeeds with probability at least
$\frac12$, and bracket refinement certifies a stationary point.
Lemma~\ref{lmm:derivative-interpolation} gives query bounds
$O_{r,\beta_r}(\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}})$ and
$O_{r,\beta_r}(\varepsilon^{-1})$.
Normalization and minimization over $r$ give the theorem.
The proof is deferred to Appendix~\ref{app:derivative-only-upper}.
head: environment

label: thm:randomized-full-jet-lower-bound
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: \bf Randomized lower bound

label: lmm:randomized-hard-family
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lmm:randomized-hard-family}
For a sufficiently large $K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}$, depending only on
$p$ and $\boldsymbol\beta$, the family above has the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, parsep=0pt]
    \item \textbf{Regularity and initial gap.}
    Every $f_j$ is $C^\infty$ and bounded below, with
    $[f_j^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}\le1$ for $1\le r\le p$ and
    $f_j(0)-\inf f_j\le\frac1{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}\le1$.
    Moreover, $f_j'(0)=-\frac{\delta}{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}
    \le-2\varepsilon$.

    \item \textbf{Indistinguishability.}
    For every fixed $x\in\mathbb R$, the response
    $\mathcal O_{f_j}^{0:p}(x)$ takes at most three distinct values
    as $j\in[m]$ varies.

    \item \textbf{Localization of stationary points.}
    For every $j\in[m]$,
    \[
    |f_j'(x)|<\varepsilon
    \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
    x\in\bigcup_{k=0}^{\infty}(j-1+km,j+km).
    \]
        These sets are pairwise disjoint for distinct $j$, so no point is
    $\varepsilon$-stationary for two different indices.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: \bf Properties of the hard family

title: Proof
body_md:
In the normalized setting $L_1=\cdots=L_p=\Delta=1$,
Lemma~\ref{lmm:randomized-hard-family} gives
$m=\Theta_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}(1/\varepsilon)$ admissible instances
with disjoint stationary sets and at most three replies per query.

Fix the entire random seed of an algorithm using at most $N$ queries.
Its decision tree has at most $3^N$ output leaves.
By localization, each leaf succeeds on at most one instance.
Averaging over the seed therefore gives
\[
\frac12
\le\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m
\mathbb P\{\text{success on }f_j\}
\le\frac{3^N}{m}.
\]
Hence $N\ge\frac{\log(m/2)}{\log3}
=\Omega_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}(\log(1/\varepsilon))$.
For general parameters, apply Lemma~\ref{lmm:normal} at an index minimizing
$L_r^{\frac1{\nu_r}}\Delta^{\frac{\nu_r-1}{\nu_r}}$.
All normalized H\"older bounds are then at least $1$, so the same hard family
is admissible. The full proof is deferred to
Appendix~\ref{app:randomized-full-jet-lower-bound}.

label: thm:deterministic-zeroth-order-upper
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: \bf Deterministic function-value upper bound

title: Algorithm
body_md:
Fix $r\in\mathcal I$ and write $\nu:=r+\beta_r$.
By Lemma~\ref{lmm:normal}, we work with
$[f^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}\le1$, $f(0)-\inf f\le1$, and
$0<\varepsilon\le1$. We first record a function-value approximation lemma.
Its proof is deferred to Appendix~\ref{app:value-interpolation}.
head: manual

label: lmm:value-interpolation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lmm:value-interpolation}
                                                               
There exists a constant $a_r\ge1$, depending only on $r$, such that,
given an interval $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, a deterministic algorithm
uses $O_r(1)$ function-value queries to construct a polynomial
$\mathsf Q_I$ satisfying
\[
\|f'-\mathsf Q_I'\|_{\infty,I}\le a_r|I|^{\nu-1},
\qquad
\mathsf Q_I(a)=f(a),\quad \mathsf Q_I(b)=f(b).
\]
head: environment
name: \bf Function-value approximation

title: Proof
body_md:
The initial gap gives
$\frac{f(4/\varepsilon)-f(0)}{4/\varepsilon}
\ge-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}$.
Each iteration preserves $D(a)<-\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$ and either
$D(b)>\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$ or this secant lower bound.
The estimate error certifies the endpoint signs, and the parent
secant is the average of the two half-interval secants.
Thus the appropriate half retains a certificate while its length halves.

At length at most $h_\varepsilon$, the value interpolant satisfies
$\|\mathsf Q_{[a,b]}'-f'\|_\infty\le\frac{\varepsilon}{8}$.
Its derivative is at most $-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ at $a$
and either at least $\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ at $b$ or has average
at least $-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}$.
Hence it crosses $-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$, yielding
$|f'(z)|\le\frac{5\varepsilon}{8}<\varepsilon$.
Each iteration uses $O_r(1)$ function-value queries, and the number
of iterations is $O_{r,\beta_r}(1+\log(1/\varepsilon))$.
Normalization, with accuracy capped at $1$, and minimization over $r$
give the theorem.
The full proof is deferred to Appendix~\ref{app:function-value-upper}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Define $g(x):=f(sx)/\Delta$. For every $r\in\mathcal I$,
\[
[g^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}
=
\frac{s^{r+\beta_r}}{\Delta}[f^{(r)}]_{\beta_r},
\qquad
g(0)-\inf g
=
\frac{f(0)-\inf f}{\Delta}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
f\in\mathcal F_{\mathcal I,\boldsymbol\beta}(\mathbf L,\Delta)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
g\in\mathcal F_{\mathcal I,\boldsymbol\beta}
(\widehat{\mathbf L},1),
\]
with inverse $f(y)=\Delta g(y/s)$.

For $0\le r\le p$, with $f^{(0)}:=f$ and $g^{(0)}:=g$,
\[
g^{(r)}(x)=\frac{s^r}{\Delta}f^{(r)}(sx),
\qquad
f^{(r)}(y)=\frac{\Delta}{s^r}g^{(r)}(y/s).
\]
Thus each oracle query can be simulated by one query in either
direction. Moreover,
\[
|g'(x)|<\frac{s\varepsilon}{\Delta}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
|f'(sx)|<\varepsilon,
\qquad
\frac{s\varepsilon}{\Delta}
=
\frac{\varepsilon}
{L_p^{1/\nu_p}\Delta^{(\nu_p-1)/\nu_p}}.
\]
The two reductions preserve query counts and success probabilities,
proving the claimed equality.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $(2K\varepsilon)^{-1}\ge4$ and
$\lfloor t\rfloor\ge t/2$ for $t\ge2$,
\[
m\ge\max\left\{4,\frac{1}{4K\varepsilon}\right\},
\qquad
2K\varepsilon\le\delta=\frac1m\le\frac14.
\]

\paragraph{Regularity and initial gap.}
The endpoint identities for $\eta_p$ and the equality $\delta m=1$
ensure matching values and derivatives through order $p$ at every
junction, including the origin. Thus $f_j\in C^p(\mathbb R)$.
On $[0,m]$, we have $1-\delta x\ge0$ and $\eta_p\ge0$;
on $(-\infty,0]$, we have $Kf_j(x)=1-\delta x\ge1$.
Periodicity therefore gives
\[
f_j\ge0,
\qquad
f_j(0)-\inf f_j\le f_j(0)=\frac1K\le1.
\]

Fix $r\in\mathcal I$.
The function
$f_j^{(r)}+\frac{\delta}{K}\mathbf1_{\{r=1\}}$
is zero outside $H_j$ and a translate of $\eta_p^{(r)}/K$
on each hidden interval. Hence
\[
\left\|
f_j^{(r)}+\frac{\delta}{K}\mathbf1_{\{r=1\}}
\right\|_\infty
\le\frac{\|\eta_p^{(r)}\|_{\infty,[0,1]}}{K}
\le\frac12.
\]
Each piece is Lipschitz with constant at most
$\|\eta_p^{(r+1)}\|_{\infty,[0,1]}/K\le1/2$.
Continuity allows these bounds to be summed across the finitely
many junctions between any $x,y\in\mathbb R$. Consequently,
\[
|f_j^{(r)}(x)-f_j^{(r)}(y)|
\le\min\left\{\frac{|x-y|}{2},1\right\}
\le |x-y|^{\beta_r}.
\]
The last inequality follows by considering $|x-y|\le1$ and
$|x-y|>1$ separately.
Thus $[f_j^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}\le1$ for every $r\in\mathcal I$,
proving $f_j\in\mathcal F_{\mathcal I,\boldsymbol\beta}(\mathbf1,1)$.

\paragraph{Indistinguishability.}
The construction and the endpoint identities give
\[
x\notin H_j
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
f_j'(x)=-\frac{\delta}{K},
\qquad
f_j^{(r)}(x)=0\quad(2\le r\le p).
\]
Hence $\mathcal O_{f_j}^{1:p}(x)=(-\delta/K,0,\ldots,0)$
outside $H_j$, with $\delta/K\ge2\varepsilon$.

\paragraph{Localization of stationary points.}
The preceding identity and the definition of $H_j$ imply
\[
\{x:|f_j'(x)|<\varepsilon\}\subseteq H_j,
\qquad
H_i\cap H_j=\varnothing\quad(i\ne j).
\]
Moreover,
\[
f_j'(j-1)=f_j'(j)=-\frac{\delta}{K}<0,
\qquad
\int_{j-1}^{j}f_j'(x)\,dx=\frac{1-\delta}{K}>0.
\]
Thus $f_j'$ is positive somewhere in $(j-1,j)$.
Continuity gives a zero on either side of that point, and
periodicity yields stationary points in every component of $H_j$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $c_p:=(16K)^{-1}$ and
\[
b:=
\max_{r\in\mathcal I}
\left(\frac{\Delta}{L_r}\right)^{\frac{1}{r+\beta_r}},
\qquad
S=\frac{\Delta}{b},
\qquad
\widehat\varepsilon:=\frac{\varepsilon}{S}.
\]
Since $\varepsilon\le c_pS$, we have
$\widehat\varepsilon\le(8K)^{-1}$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:hard-family-properties} with accuracy
$\widehat\varepsilon$, and define $F_j(x):=\Delta f_j(x/b)$.

\paragraph{Rescaling.}
For $1\le r\le p$, the chain rule gives
$F_j^{(r)}(x)=\Delta b^{-r}f_j^{(r)}(x/b)$.
Consequently, for every $r\in\mathcal I$,
\[
[F_j^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}
=
\frac{\Delta}{b^{r+\beta_r}}[f_j^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}
\le
\frac{\Delta}{b^{r+\beta_r}}
\le L_r,
\qquad
F_j(0)-\inf F_j
=
\Delta\bigl(f_j(0)-\inf f_j\bigr)
\le\Delta.
\]
Thus $F_j\in\mathcal F_{\mathcal I,\boldsymbol\beta}
(\mathbf L,\Delta)$.
Since $F_j'(x)=Sf_j'(x/b)$, a point $x$ is
$\varepsilon$-stationary for $F_j$ if and only if $x/b$ is
$\widehat\varepsilon$-stationary for $f_j$.
Every successful output therefore belongs to $bH_j$, and these
sets are pairwise disjoint.
Furthermore, outside $bH_j$, the oracle returns the common response
\[
\mathcal O_{F_j}^{1:p}(x)
=
v:=\left(-\frac{S\delta}{K},0,\ldots,0\right).
\]

\paragraph{Query counting.}
Let $A$ use at most $N$ queries on every run.
The case $N\ge m$ is immediate, so assume $N<m$.
Fix a random seed $r$ and run $A$ with the constant response $v$.
This execution terminates within $N$ queries, since its first
$N$ responses remain consistent with at least $m-N>0$ instances.

Let $Q_r$ be the set of indices whose regions $bH_j$ are queried,
and let $\bar x_r$ be the output.
Then $|Q_r|\le N$, and indistinguishability gives
$\widehat x_A(F_j;r)=\bar x_r$ for every $j\notin Q_r$.
By localization and disjointness,
\[
\sum_{j=1}^m
\mathbf 1\!\left\{
    |F_j'(\widehat x_A(F_j;r))|<\varepsilon
\right\}
\le
|Q_r|+
\sum_{j\notin Q_r}\mathbf 1\{\bar x_r\in bH_j\}
\le N+1.
\]
Averaging over the random seed and using the success guarantee,
\[
\frac12
\le
\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m
\mathbb P\!\left(
    |F_j'(\widehat x_A(F_j))|<\varepsilon
\right)
\le\frac{N+1}{m}.
\]
Since $m\ge4$ and $m\ge(4K\widehat\varepsilon)^{-1}$,
\[
N\ge\frac m2-1
\ge\frac m4
\ge\frac{1}{16K\widehat\varepsilon}
=c_p\frac{S}{\varepsilon}.
\]
The bound holds for $\mathcal O^{1:p}$ and therefore also
for $\mathcal O^1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\varphi$ is fixed, choose
\[
M_p:=\max_{0\le k\le p}
\|\varphi^{(k)}\|_{L^1(\mathbb R)}\in[1,\infty),
\qquad
K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\ge
\max_{1\le r\le p}(4M_p)^{\frac1{\nu_r-1}}.
\]

\noindent\textbf{Regularity and initial gap.}
Smoothness and compact support of the kernel give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\psi_S\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R),\qquad
  \operatorname{supp}\psi_S\subset E_S+[-\frac h2,\frac h2],\\
&0\le\psi_S(x)
  =\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbf1_{E_S}(x-t)\varphi_h(t)\,dt
  \le\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi_h(t)\,dt=1,\\
&f_S\in C^\infty(\mathbb R),\qquad f_S(0)=\Delta,\qquad
  f_S'=-2\varepsilon\psi_S\le0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $f_S$ is nonincreasing, constant on both tails, and bounded below.
For $0\le k\le p$, differentiation and scaling yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
\varphi_h^{(k)}(t)
  &=\frac1{h^{k+1}}\varphi^{(k)}(\frac th),
&\|\varphi_h^{(k)}\|_1
  &=h^{-k}\|\varphi^{(k)}\|_1,\\
\psi_S^{(k)}&=\mathbf1_{E_S}*\varphi_h^{(k)},
&\|\psi_S^{(k)}\|_\infty
  &\le\|\mathbf1_{E_S}\|_\infty\|\varphi_h^{(k)}\|_1
   \le M_ph^{-k}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently, for $1\le r\le p$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_S^{(r)}&=-2\varepsilon\psi_S^{(r-1)},
&f_S^{(r+1)}&=-2\varepsilon\psi_S^{(r)},\\
\|f_S^{(r)}\|_\infty&\le2\varepsilon M_ph^{-(r-1)},
&\|f_S^{(r+1)}\|_\infty&\le2\varepsilon M_ph^{-r}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For $d:=|x-y|>0$, the triangle inequality
and the mean value theorem give
\[
\begin{aligned}
|f_S^{(r)}(x)-f_S^{(r)}(y)|
&\le\min\{2\|f_S^{(r)}\|_\infty,
              \|f_S^{(r+1)}\|_\infty d\}\\
&\le\min\{4\varepsilon M_ph^{-(r-1)},
              2\varepsilon M_ph^{-r}d\}\\
&\le4\varepsilon M_ph^{-(r-1)}\min\{1,\frac dh\}\\
&\le4\varepsilon M_ph^{-(\nu_r-1)}d^{\beta_r},
\end{aligned}
\]
where $\min\{1,t\}\le t^{\beta_r}$ for $t\ge0$ and
$0<\beta_r\le1$.
Since $h^{\nu_r-1}\ge
K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}^{\nu_r-1}\frac{\varepsilon}{L_r}$,
\[
[f_S^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}
\le4M_p\varepsilon h^{-(\nu_r-1)}
\le\frac{4M_p}{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}^{\nu_r-1}}L_r
\le L_r.
\]
Tonelli's theorem gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_S(x)\,dx
&=\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi_h(t)
  \left(\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbf1_{E_S}(x-t)\,dx\right)dt\\
&=|E_S|\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi_h(t)\,dt
 =|E_S|\le2h|S|.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because the right-tail value of $f_S$ equals its infimum,
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_S(0)-\inf f_S
&=2\varepsilon\int_0^\infty\psi_S(t)\,dt\\
&\le2\varepsilon\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_S(t)\,dt
 \le4\varepsilon h|S|\le\Delta.
\end{aligned}
\]

\noindent\textbf{Oracle values.}
For $s\in S$, $|x-s|<\frac h2$, and
$t\in\operatorname{supp}\varphi_h$,
\[
|x-t-s|\le|x-s|+|t|<\frac h2+\frac h2=h,
\qquad x-t\in[s-h,s+h]\subset E_S.
\]
Consequently, throughout $(s-\frac h2,s+\frac h2)$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\psi_S(x)
&=\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbf1_{E_S}(x-t)\varphi_h(t)\,dt
 =\int_{\mathbb R}\varphi_h(t)\,dt=1,\\
f_S'(x)&=-2\varepsilon,\qquad
f_S^{(j)}(x)=-2\varepsilon\psi_S^{(j-1)}(x)=0
\quad(2\le j\le p).
\end{aligned}
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Take the constant in the theorem small enough that
$c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\le\frac1{16K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}$.
For every $1\le r\le p$, the accuracy assumption gives
$\varepsilon\le c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}
L_r^{\frac1{\nu_r}}\Delta^{\frac{\nu_r-1}{\nu_r}}$.
Since $\frac{\nu_r}{\nu_r-1}>1$ and
$0<c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}<1$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\varepsilon^{\frac{\nu_r}{\nu_r-1}}L_r^{-\frac1{\nu_r-1}}
&\le c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}^{\frac{\nu_r}{\nu_r-1}}\Delta
 \le c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\Delta
 \le\frac{\Delta}{16K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}},\\
\varepsilon h
&=K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\max_{1\le r\le p}
  \varepsilon^{\frac{\nu_r}{\nu_r-1}}L_r^{-\frac1{\nu_r-1}}
 \le\frac{\Delta}{16}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Suppose a correct deterministic algorithm has worst-case query budget
$Q<\frac{\Delta}{16\varepsilon h}$.
Simulate it by reporting $f'(x)=-2\varepsilon$ and
$f^{(j)}(x)=0$ for $2\le j\le p$ at every query.
If it outputs within $Q$ queries, let $S$ contain the origin,
all query locations, and its output $\widehat x$.
If it requests query $Q+1$, let $S$ contain the origin and the
first $Q+1$ query locations.
In either case, $0\in S$, $|S|\le Q+2$, and
\[
4\varepsilon h|S|
\le4\varepsilon h(Q+2)
<\frac{\Delta}{4}+8\varepsilon h
\le\frac{3\Delta}{4}<\Delta.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lmm:derivative-hard-family} therefore supplies an admissible
$f_S\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ satisfying
\[
f_S'(s)=-2\varepsilon,\qquad
f_S^{(j)}(s)=0
\quad(s\in S,\ 2\le j\le p).
\]

Matching oracle replies and determinism reproduce the simulation
on $f_S$ inductively.
Thus the algorithm either outputs $\widehat x\in S$ with
$|f_S'(\widehat x)|=2\varepsilon>\varepsilon$, or requests query
$Q+1$, contradicting correctness or the query budget.
Nontermination is likewise impossible: taking $S$ to contain the origin
and the at most $Q$ queried points, the corresponding admissible $f_S$
reproduces the same nonterminating execution.

Hence every correct algorithm needs at least
\[
\frac{\Delta}{16\varepsilon h}
=\frac1{16K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}
\min_{1\le r\le p}
L_r^{\frac1{\nu_r-1}}\Delta
\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu_r}{\nu_r-1}}
\]
queries. Since $c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\le\frac1{16K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}$,
this proves the stated bound; moreover, $0\in S$ gives
$f_S'(0)=-2\varepsilon$.

label: eq:derivative-upper-integral
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $r\in\mathcal I$ and write $\nu:=r+\beta_r$.
We first assume $[f^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}\le1$,
$f(0)-\inf f\le1$, and $0<\varepsilon\le1$.
The initial query either returns an $\varepsilon$-stationary point
or, after reflection if necessary, gives $f'(0)\le-\varepsilon$.
Reflection preserves the smoothness conditions and initial gap.
Set $T:=\frac{2}{\varepsilon}$.
The fundamental theorem of calculus and the gap bound give
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:derivative-upper-integral}
\int_0^T f'(x)\,dx=f(T)-f(0)\ge-1,
\qquad
\int_0^T(f'(x)+\varepsilon)\,dx\ge1.
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Deterministic algorithm.}
Let $P$ be the approximation with error $\frac{\varepsilon}{8}$.
By Eq.~\eqref{eq:derivative-upper-integral},
\[
\frac1T\int_0^T P(x)\,dx
\ge-\frac1T-\frac{\varepsilon}{8}
=-\frac{5\varepsilon}{8}.
\]
Thus $P$ attains a value strictly above $-\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$.
Since $P(0)=f'(0)\le-\varepsilon$ and $P$ is continuous,
it crosses this level.
Every such crossing $z$ satisfies
\[
|f'(z)|
\le |P(z)|+\frac{\varepsilon}{8}
=\frac{7\varepsilon}{8}<\varepsilon.
\]
A crossing can be found from the polynomial pieces without further
oracle queries.
Including the initial query, Lemma~\ref{lmm:derivative-interpolation}
bounds the deterministic query count by
\[
O_{r,\beta_r}\!\left(
1+T\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{8}\right)^{-\frac1{\nu-1}}
\right)
=O_{r,\beta_r}\!\left(\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}\right).
\]

\paragraph{Randomized algorithm.}
Now let $P$ have error $1$, and set
$w:=(P+1+\varepsilon)_+$ and
$G:=\{x\in[0,T]:f'(x)>-\varepsilon\}$.
Since $w\ge(f'+\varepsilon)_+$,
\[
A:=\int_G w(x)\,dx
\ge\int_G(f'(x)+\varepsilon)\,dx
\ge\int_0^T(f'(x)+\varepsilon)\,dx
\ge1.
\]
On $G^c$, the approximation bound gives
$P+1+\varepsilon\le f'+2+\varepsilon\le2$.
Hence $B:=\int_{G^c}w(x)\,dx\le2T$.
In particular, $W:=A+B>0$, and sampling from $\rho:=\frac{w}{W}$
gives
\[
\mathbb P(X\in G)
=\frac{A}{A+B}
\ge\frac1{1+2T}
=\frac1{1+4/\varepsilon}.
\]
The density is determined by the known polynomial pieces;
its integral and samples require no additional oracle queries.
For $N:=\left\lceil(1+\frac4\varepsilon)\log2\right\rceil$
independent samples,
\[
\mathbb P(\text{all $N$ samples miss }G)
\le\left(1-\frac1{1+4/\varepsilon}\right)^N
\le\exp\!\left(-\frac{N}{1+4/\varepsilon}\right)
\le\frac12.
\]
Every hit either satisfies $|f'(X)|<\varepsilon$
or has $f'(X)\ge\varepsilon$, yielding a sign bracket with the origin.

\paragraph{Bracket refinement and query count.}
Bisection either returns an $\varepsilon$-stationary point
or preserves $f'(a)\le-\varepsilon$ and $f'(b)\ge\varepsilon$.
Starting from length at most $T$, it reaches
$b-a\le h_\varepsilon:=\varepsilon^{\frac1{\nu-1}}$
within
\[
\left\lceil\log_2\left(\frac{T}{h_\varepsilon}\right)\right\rceil
=O_{r,\beta_r}(1+\log(\varepsilon^{-1}))
\]
queries.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lmm:derivative-interpolation} on this interval
with error $\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$.
The resulting continuous piecewise polynomial $Q$ satisfies
$Q(a)=f'(a)<0<f'(b)=Q(b)$, so it has a root $z$.
Every root satisfies
$|f'(z)|\le\frac{\varepsilon}{2}<\varepsilon$.
The terminal approximation uses
\[
O_{r,\beta_r}\!\left(
1+(b-a)\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\right)^{-\frac1{\nu-1}}
\right)=O_{r,\beta_r}(1)
\]
queries.
Thus every hit of $G$ leads to a valid output.
The initial query, coarse approximation, at most $N$ samples,
and at most one bracket refinement together use
$O_{r,\beta_r}(\varepsilon^{-1})$ queries on every execution,
since $0<\varepsilon\le1$.
The success probability is at least $\frac12$.

\paragraph{General parameters.}
By Lemma~\ref{lmm:normal}, the normalized accuracy is
\[
\widehat\varepsilon
:=\frac{\varepsilon}
{L_r^{\frac1\nu}\Delta^{\frac{\nu-1}{\nu}}}.
\]
The theorem's assumption ensures $0<\widehat\varepsilon\le1$.
The algorithms use only the selected smoothness condition,
so the other normalized conditions impose no restriction on the argument.
Substituting $\widehat\varepsilon$ into the two normalized query bounds
gives, respectively,
\[
O_{r,\beta_r}\!\left(
L_r^{\frac1{\nu-1}}\Delta
\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}\right),
\qquad
O_{r,\beta_r}\!\left(
L_r^{\frac1\nu}\Delta^{\frac{\nu-1}{\nu}}\varepsilon^{-1}\right).
\]
Normalization preserves query counts and success probabilities.
Taking the maximum of the constants over $r\in\mathcal I$
and minimizing each bound over $r$ proves the theorem.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\beta:=\beta_r$ and $\alpha:=\nu-1=r-1+\beta>0$.
If $a=b$, one derivative query gives the constant polynomial
$P_\delta\equiv f'(a)$, which satisfies all the required properties.
Henceforth assume $a<b$.

For a subinterval $J=[c,d]\subseteq I$, let $R_J$ be the
degree-$(r-1)$ Taylor polynomial of $f'$ at $c$.
If $r=1$, then $R_J\equiv f'(c)$, and Hölder continuity gives
$\|f'-R_J\|_{\infty,J}\le |J|^\beta$.
If $r\ge2$, the integral Taylor formula gives
\[
f'(x)-R_J(x)
=
\frac{1}{(r-2)!}
\int_c^x
(x-t)^{r-2}
\bigl(f^{(r)}(t)-f^{(r)}(c)\bigr)\,dt.
\]
Since $[f^{(r)}]_\beta\le1$, the absolute value of the difference
inside the integral is at most $|J|^\beta$.
Integrating the kernel therefore yields
$|f'(x)-R_J(x)|
\le \frac{|J|^\beta(x-c)^{r-1}}{(r-1)!}
\le \frac{|J|^\alpha}{(r-1)!}$.
Thus, for every $r\ge1$,
$\|f'-R_J\|_{\infty,J}
\le \frac{|J|^\alpha}{(r-1)!}$.

Let $q:=\max\{r,2\}$, and let $\mathsf P_J$ interpolate $f'$
at $q$ equally spaced nodes of $J$, including both endpoints.
Let $\Lambda_q$ be the Lebesgue constant of these nodes.
It depends only on $q$, since affine changes of the interval
preserve the interpolation operator norm.
The interpolation operator has norm $\Lambda_q$ and reproduces
$R_J$, whose degree is at most $q-1$.
Applying it to $f'-R_J$ and using the triangle inequality gives
\[
\|f'-\mathsf P_J\|_{\infty,J}
\le
(1+\Lambda_q)\|f'-R_J\|_{\infty,J}
\le a_r|J|^\alpha,
\]
where
$a_r:=\max\left\{1,\frac{1+\Lambda_q}{(r-1)!}\right\}$.
This argument also covers $r=1$, since the two-node interpolant
reproduces the constant polynomial $R_J$.

Set
$h_\delta:=\left(\frac{\delta}{a_r}\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}$
and $n:=\left\lceil\frac{|I|}{h_\delta}\right\rceil$.
Partition $I$ into $n$ equal intervals and construct
$\mathsf P_J$ on each interval using derivative queries.
Adjacent interpolants agree with $f'$ at their common endpoint,
so the resulting piecewise polynomial $P_\delta$ is continuous.
The same endpoint interpolation gives
$P_\delta(a)=f'(a)$ and $P_\delta(b)=f'(b)$.
Every mesh interval has length at most $h_\delta$, and hence
$\|f'-P_\delta\|_{\infty,I}
\le a_rh_\delta^\alpha=\delta$.

Finally, each interval requires at most $q$ derivative queries.
The total number is therefore at most
\[
qn
\le
q\left(
1+a_r^{\frac{1}{\alpha}}|I|
\delta^{-\frac{1}{\alpha}}
\right)
=
O_{r,\beta_r}\!\left(
1+|I|\delta^{-\frac{1}{\nu-1}}
\right).
\]
All query locations are deterministic.
The Taylor polynomials are used only in the error analysis;
the construction queries only $f'$ at the interpolation nodes.

title: Proof
body_md:
The fixed kernel gives $\Phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$,
$0\le\Phi\le1$, and $\Phi^{(q)}=0$ outside $(0,1)$ for every $q\ge1$.
In particular, all positive-order derivatives of $\Phi$ are bounded.
Choose
\[
K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\ge
\max\left\{1,
\max_{1\le r\le p}2\|\Phi^{(r)}\|_\infty,
\max_{1\le r\le p}\|\Phi^{(r+1)}\|_\infty\right\}.
\]
The accuracy assumption gives $m\ge2$, while the definition of $m$
gives $\delta m=1$ and $\delta\ge2K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\varepsilon$.

\noindent\textbf{Regularity and initial gap.}
Since $1-j\le0$ and $m-j+1\ge1$, the endpoint values on the base period are
$f_j(0)=f_j(m)=\frac1{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}$.
Moreover, $f_j'(0)=f_j'(m)=-\frac{\delta}{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}$
and $f_j^{(q)}(0)=f_j^{(q)}(m)=0$ for every $q\ge2$.
Thus the periodic extension matches in every derivative at each multiple
of $m$. The same values and derivatives match the linear extension at $0$,
so $f_j\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$.

On $[0,m]$, both $1-\delta x$ and $\Phi(x-j+1)$ are nonnegative and
on $(-\infty,0]$, $f_j(x)\ge\frac1{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}$.
Periodicity therefore gives $f_j\ge0$ on $\mathbb R$, and hence
$f_j(0)-\inf f_j\le\frac1{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}\le1$.
Also, $f_j'(0)=-\frac{\delta}{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}\le-2\varepsilon$.

Fix $1\le r\le p$.
The nonconstant part of $f_j^{(r)}$ consists of translates of
$\frac{\Phi^{(r)}}{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}$ on the disjoint hidden intervals
and is zero elsewhere. Its oscillation is therefore at most
$\frac{2\|\Phi^{(r)}\|_\infty}{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}$.
Smooth gluing also gives
$\|f_j^{(r+1)}\|_\infty\le
\frac{\|\Phi^{(r+1)}\|_\infty}{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}$.
For $d:=|x-y|>0$, these two bounds imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
|f_j^{(r)}(x)-f_j^{(r)}(y)|
&\le\min\left\{
\frac{2\|\Phi^{(r)}\|_\infty}{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}},
\frac{\|\Phi^{(r+1)}\|_\infty}{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}d
\right\}\\
&\le\min\{1,d\}\le d^{\beta_r}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last inequality follows from $d\le d^{\beta_r}$ when $d\le1$
and $1\le d^{\beta_r}$ when $d\ge1$.
Dividing by $d^{\beta_r}$ and taking the supremum gives
$[f_j^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}\le1$.

\noindent\textbf{Indistinguishability.}
For $x\le0$, all functions have the same linear jet, so the oracle response
is independent of $j$.
For $x>0$, let $t:=x-m\lfloor x/m\rfloor\in[0,m)$ and
$\ell:=1+\lfloor t\rfloor\in[m]$.
If $j>\ell$, then $t-j+1\le0$; if $j<\ell$, then $t-j+1\ge1$.
Consequently,
\[
f_j(x)=\frac1{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}
\begin{cases}
1-\delta t, & j>\ell,\\
2-\delta t, & j<\ell,\\
1-\delta t+\Phi(t-\ell+1), & j=\ell.
\end{cases}
\]
For $j\ne\ell$, the positive-order derivatives of the step vanish, giving
$f_j'(x)=-\frac{\delta}{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}$ and
$f_j^{(r)}(x)=0$ for $2\le r\le p$.
Thus all indices $j>\ell$ give one common full response, and all indices
$j<\ell$ give another. The single remaining index $j=\ell$ contributes
at most one additional response.
At an integer residue, the flat endpoint derivatives make this transition
response coincide with a linear response.
Hence every fixed query has at most three possible full responses,
including at the interval and period boundaries.

\noindent\textbf{Localization of stationary points.}
Outside the open copies $(j-1+km,j+km)$, $k\ge0$, the step derivative
vanishes, including at their endpoints. The negative linear extension
has the same derivative, so every such point satisfies
$f_j'(x)=-\frac{\delta}{K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}\le-2\varepsilon$.
It therefore cannot be $\varepsilon$-stationary.

Finally, these open unit intervals have integer left endpoints.
If copies associated with $j$ and $j'$ intersect, their left endpoints
must agree, giving $j-j'=(k'-k)m$.
Since $|j-j'|\le m-1$, this implies $j=j'$.
Thus a stationary point lies in copies associated with exactly one index.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}$ as in Lemma~\ref{lmm:randomized-hard-family}.
Choose the theorem constant sufficiently small that
$c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\le\frac1{64K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}^2}$
and $c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\le\frac1{2\log3}$.

\noindent\textbf{Normalized parameters.}
Suppose $L_1=\cdots=L_p=\Delta=1$ and
$0<\varepsilon\le c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}$.
Then $\varepsilon\le\frac1{4K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}}$, so the hard family
is admissible by Lemma~\ref{lmm:randomized-hard-family}.
Since $\frac1{2K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\varepsilon}\ge2$, its size satisfies
\[
m=\left\lfloor\frac1{2K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\varepsilon}\right\rfloor
\ge\frac1{2K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\varepsilon}-1
\ge\frac1{4K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\varepsilon}.
\]

Consider any randomized algorithm using at most $N$ queries per execution
and succeeding with probability at least $\frac12$ on every admissible input.
Let $J$ be uniform on $[m]$, independently of the algorithm's random seed $U$,
and run the algorithm on $f_J$.
Fix the entire random seed, including any randomness used to choose the output.
Each query is then determined by the preceding replies, and each query node
has at most three children by the indistinguishability property.

There are at most $3^N$ output leaves.
Indeed, a depth-zero tree has at most one output leaf, and each of the
at most three subtrees of a query node has remaining depth at most $N-1$.
Induction gives the bound. Stopping before depth $N$ is allowed in this
argument, and a nonterminating branch contributes no output leaf.
Each output leaf has a fixed point. By localization, that point is
$\varepsilon$-stationary for at most one index $j$, whether or not it was
queried. Thus, for each fixed seed, the algorithm succeeds on at most
$3^N$ members of the family.

Since $J$ is uniform and independent of $U$, averaging over the seed bounds
the success probability by $\frac{3^N}{m}$.
The success guarantee on every $f_j$ bounds the same probability below by
$\frac12$. Therefore,
\[
\frac12
\le\mathbb P\{\text{success}\}
\le\frac{3^N}{m},
\qquad
N\ge\frac{\log(m/2)}{\log3}
\ge\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)-\log(8K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta})}{\log3}.
\]
Our choice of $c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}$ ensures
$\log(1/\varepsilon)\ge2\log(8K_{p,\boldsymbol\beta})$.
Consequently, $N\ge\frac1{2\log3}\log(1/\varepsilon)$,
and the choice of $c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}$ gives
$N\ge c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\log(1/\varepsilon)$.

\noindent\textbf{General parameters.}
Choose $r_*$ attaining the minimum of
$L_r^{\frac1{\nu_r}}\Delta^{\frac{\nu_r-1}{\nu_r}}$
over $1\le r\le p$, and set
$s:=\left(\frac{\Delta}{L_{r_*}}\right)^{\frac1{\nu_{r_*}}}$
as in Lemma~\ref{lmm:normal}.
For every $1\le r\le p$, the normalized bounds satisfy
\[
\widehat L_r=\frac{L_rs^{\nu_r}}{\Delta}
=\left(
\frac{L_r^{\frac1{\nu_r}}\Delta^{\frac{\nu_r-1}{\nu_r}}}
{L_{r_*}^{\frac1{\nu_{r_*}}}
\Delta^{\frac{\nu_{r_*}-1}{\nu_{r_*}}}}
\right)^{\nu_r}\ge1.
\]
Hence the normalized class contains the unit-parameter hard family.
Its normalized accuracy is
\[
\widehat\varepsilon=\frac{s\varepsilon}{\Delta}
=\frac{\varepsilon}
{\displaystyle\min_{1\le r\le p}
L_r^{\frac1{\nu_r}}\Delta^{\frac{\nu_r-1}{\nu_r}}}
\le c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}.
\]
Any algorithm correct on the normalized class must therefore satisfy
the preceding lower bound at accuracy $\widehat\varepsilon$.
Lemma~\ref{lmm:normal} preserves the query count and success probability,
so the original class also requires at least
$c_{p,\boldsymbol\beta}\log(1/\widehat\varepsilon)$ queries.
Substituting the displayed accuracy proves the theorem.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\nu:=r+\beta_r$ and set $q:=\max\{r+1,3\}$.
Construct $\mathsf Q_I$ by interpolation at $q$ equally spaced
nodes of $I$, including both endpoints.
Let $I=[a,b]$, $H:=b-a$, and let $R$ be the degree-$r$
Taylor polynomial of $f$ at $a$.
Taylor's integral remainder and
$|f^{(r)}(t)-f^{(r)}(a)|\le H^{\beta_r}$ give
\[
\|f-R\|_{\infty,I}\le\frac{H^\nu}{r!},
\qquad
\|f'-R'\|_{\infty,I}
\le\frac{H^{\nu-1}}{(r-1)!}.
\]
For the first estimate, the remainder is
$\frac{1}{(r-1)!}\int_a^x
(x-t)^{r-1}(f^{(r)}(t)-f^{(r)}(a))\,dt$.
The second follows from the analogous formula for $f'$ when $r\ge2$;
when $r=1$, it is precisely the H\"older bound on $f'$.

Let $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_q$ be the Lagrange basis polynomials
for the chosen nodes on $[0,1]$, and set
$\Gamma_q:=\sum_{j=1}^q\|\ell_j'\|_{\infty,[0,1]}$.
Since $q-1\ge r$, interpolation reproduces $R$.
After rescaling $I$ to $[0,1]$, the derivative of the interpolation
operator has norm at most $\frac{\Gamma_q}{H}$.
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathsf Q_I'-f'\|_{\infty,I}
&\le \|R'-f'\|_{\infty,I}
   +\|(\mathsf Q_I-R)'\|_{\infty,I}\\
&\le \frac{H^{\nu-1}}{(r-1)!}
   +\frac{\Gamma_q}{H}\|f-R\|_{\infty,I}\\
&\le \left(\frac{1}{(r-1)!}
   +\frac{\Gamma_q}{r!}\right)H^{\nu-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $\|f'-\mathsf Q_I'\|_{\infty,I}\le a_r|I|^{\nu-1}$ holds with
$a_r:=\max\{1,\frac{1}{(r-1)!}+\frac{\Gamma_q}{r!}\}$.
Endpoint interpolation gives $\mathsf Q_I(a)=f(a)$ and
$\mathsf Q_I(b)=f(b)$.
The construction uses at most $q=O_r(1)$ function-value queries.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $r\in\mathcal I$ and write $\nu:=r+\beta_r$.
We first assume $[f^{(r)}]_{\beta_r}\le1$,
$f(0)-\inf f\le1$, and $0<\varepsilon\le1$.

\noindent\textbf{Derivative estimates.}
Lemma~\ref{lmm:value-interpolation} on an interval of length
$h_\varepsilon$ gives $|D(x)-f'(x)|\le\frac{\varepsilon}{8}$
at either endpoint.
It also gives the required uniform bound for the terminal interpolant.

Whenever $|D(x)|\le\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$, the returned point satisfies
$|f'(x)|\le\frac{7\varepsilon}{8}<\varepsilon$.
Otherwise, $D(x)<-\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$ implies
$f'(x)<-\frac{5\varepsilon}{8}$, and
$D(x)>\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$ implies
$f'(x)>\frac{5\varepsilon}{8}$.
If the initial estimate is positive, reflection negates both
$f'(0)$ and its cached estimate, preserving their error bound.
It also preserves the H\"older condition and initial gap.
The reflected interpolation interval still has the origin as an endpoint.

\noindent\textbf{Interval invariant.}
Every active interval has
$D(a)<-\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$, both endpoint estimates lie outside
$[-\frac{3\varepsilon}{4},\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}]$, and
at least one of the certificates
\[
D(b)>\frac{3\varepsilon}{4},
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\ge-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}.
\]
Initially, $a=0$ and $b=T:=\frac{4}{\varepsilon}$.
The gap bound gives $f(T)-f(0)\ge-1$, hence the secant certificate.
The estimate at $T$ either returns a stationary point or lies outside
the acceptance range, establishing the invariant.

Let $c:=\frac{a+b}{2}$.
An accepted estimate returns a valid point as proved above.
If $D(c)>\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$, replacing $b$ by $c$
establishes the first certificate and preserves the negative left estimate.
Otherwise, $D(c)<-\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$.
If $D(b)>\frac{3\varepsilon}{4}$, replacing $a$ by $c$
preserves both the first certificate and the negative left estimate.

In the remaining case, both $D(c)$ and $D(b)$ are negative.
The parent interval must therefore have the secant certificate.
The parent secant is the average of the two half-interval secants,
so at least one half has secant slope at least
$-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}$.
Since $c-a=b-c$, the left half has the larger slope exactly when
$2f(c)\ge f(a)+f(b)$.
The final two branches select that half, whose left endpoint is either
$a$ or $c$ and has a negative estimate.
Thus every nonreturning iteration preserves the invariant and halves
the interval length.

\noindent\textbf{Terminal output.}
Let $P:=\mathsf Q_{[a,b]}'$.
Since $b-a\le h_\varepsilon$, we have
$\|P-f'\|_{\infty,[a,b]}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{8}$.
The negative left estimate gives
$P(a)\le f'(a)+\frac{\varepsilon}{8}<-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$.
If the first certificate holds, then
$P(b)\ge f'(b)-\frac{\varepsilon}{8}>\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$.
If the secant certificate holds, endpoint interpolation gives
\[
\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b P(x)\,dx
=\frac{\mathsf Q_{[a,b]}(b)-\mathsf Q_{[a,b]}(a)}{b-a}
=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}
\ge-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}.
\]
Hence $P$ attains a value at least $-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}$.
In both cases, continuity gives a point $z\in[a,b]$ with
$P(z)=-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$.
Every such point satisfies
$|f'(z)|\le|P(z)|+\frac{\varepsilon}{8}
=\frac{5\varepsilon}{8}<\varepsilon$.
The root is computed from the known polynomial without additional
oracle queries.

\noindent\textbf{Query budget.}
Lemma~\ref{lmm:value-interpolation} gives $O_r(1)$ value queries
for each derivative estimate and for the terminal interpolant.
The loop makes at most
$\left\lceil\log_2\left(\frac{4/\varepsilon}{h_\varepsilon}\right)\right\rceil$
iterations, in addition to the two initial estimates.
The ratio in the logarithm equals
$4(8a_r)^{\frac{1}{\nu-1}}\varepsilon^{-\frac{\nu}{\nu-1}}$,
so the total is
$O_{r,\beta_r}(1+\log(1/\varepsilon))$.
Cached endpoint values suffice for every secant comparison.

\noindent\textbf{General parameters.}
Lemma~\ref{lmm:normal} gives normalized accuracy
$\widehat\varepsilon:=\frac{\varepsilon}
{L_r^{\frac{1}{\nu}}\Delta^{\frac{\nu-1}{\nu}}}$.
Run the normalized algorithm with accuracy
$\min\{\widehat\varepsilon,1\}$.
Its output also meets accuracy $\widehat\varepsilon$.
Each normalized function-value query is simulated by one original
function-value query, and rescaling preserves the stationarity guarantee.
Thus, for every selected $r$, the query bound is
\[
O_{r,\beta_r}\left(
1+\log_+\left(
\frac{L_r^{\frac{1}{\nu}}\Delta^{\frac{\nu-1}{\nu}}}{\varepsilon}
\right)\right).
\]
Taking the maximum of the constants over $1\le r\le p$ and choosing
an index minimizing
$L_r^{\frac{1}{\nu_r}}\Delta^{\frac{\nu_r-1}{\nu_r}}$
proves the theorem.
